facts.text: On this date in 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen accidentally discovered X-rays in Würzburg, Germany. Within weeks, the image of his wife's hand had circled the globe — the internet moment of its era.
On this date in 1960, JFK won the presidency by just 112,827 votes out of 68 million cast — a margin of 0.17%, the second-closest popular vote in U.S. history.
Mongolia has more horses than people. With 3.5 million residents and roughly 4.2 million horses, it is the last country on Earth where the horse-to-human ratio meaningfully exceeds one.
Lagos is not Nigeria's capital — Abuja is. But Lagos holds more people than 35 individual African countries and processes roughly a quarter of the entire continent's maritime trade.
The Maldives employs a full-time ambassador whose sole job is climate diplomacy. No other nation has created a dedicated cabinet-level post for a single environmental threat to its own existence.
On this day in 1895, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 40.94. It has since multiplied roughly 1,100 times — every decade of holding rewarded patience more than genius.
On Nov 8, 1971, the National Association of Securities Dealers launched NASDAQ — the world's first electronic stock market. Floor traders called it a toy. It now lists Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon.

The Dutch East India Company, the first publicly traded corporation, paid dividends for nearly 200 consecutive years — sometimes borrowing money to do it, keeping investors happy while the empire rotted.
The S&P 500 has fallen more than 1% on a single day roughly 95 times per decade. Investors who sold on each drop and missed the 10 best days of each decade ended up poorer than those who did nothing.
Warren Buffett made approximately 97% of his net worth after his 65th birthday. Compounding is not a strategy — it is a waiting game disguised as a strategy.
On this date in 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays by accident, noticing a fluorescent glow across his lab. Within weeks, he had photographed his wife's hand, bones and all.
Your skeleton replaces itself entirely every decade. The calcium in your femur right now was not there ten years ago.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
On this date in 1656, Edmond Halley was born — the man who realized the comet bearing his name had already visited three times in recorded history, unrecognized each time.
Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of color receptors, compared to the human three. They likely do not perceive richer color — they process it faster, almost like hardware instead of software.

On this day in 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays by accident — and within a year, battlefield surgeons were using them to find bullets in soldiers. The gap between discovery and mass deployment was shorter than most iPhone upgrade cycles.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Oxford's oldest colleges date to the 1200s; Tenochtitlán wasn't founded until 1325.

On this day in 1923, Hitler's Beer Hall Putsch failed so completely that he was arrested within days. The prison sentence that followed gave him time to dictate Mein Kampf — the failure that enabled everything after.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She was born around 69 BC; the pyramid was finished around 2560 BC.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, before the light bulb. Japan was still sending faxes routinely into the 2020s.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Already feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. Neither nostalgia nor homesickness quite covers it — the language needed its own word.
On this day in 1895, Röntgen discovered X-rays. The German word he chose, Röntgenstrahlen, lost to English. What survived: the ghostly prefix of the unknown — X.
Mamihlapinatapai: a Yaghan word meaning a look shared by two people, each wishing the other would initiate something both desire. The language has one surviving native speaker.
On this day in 1793, the Louvre opened as a public museum. The French word vernissage — varnishing day, when artists touched up work before an opening — still names every debut exhibition.
On this date in 2017, Bitcoin hit $7,400 for the first time — then lost 29% within a week as the SegWit2x hard fork collapsed after its key backers publicly withdrew support.
On this date in 2021, the Ethereum London upgrade had been live for exactly three months, having burned over 1 million ETH in fees — permanently removing them from circulation.
The Bitcoin genesis block contains a hidden message: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.' Satoshi embedded it manually; it cannot be altered retroactively.
Ethereum's gas limit is not set by developers — it is voted up or down by miners (now validators) each block, making it one of the protocol's few genuinely decentralized governance mechanisms.
The most expensive single NFT transaction by gas cost was not a Bored Ape or CryptoPunk — it was a failed contract interaction in 2021 that burned $430,000 in ETH and minted nothing.
On this day in 2022, ChatGPT launched. It reached 1 million users in 5 days — faster than any consumer product in history. OpenAI had expected slow growth and nearly missed the moment.
On this day in 2016, Microsoft quietly open-sourced CNTK, its deep learning toolkit. It was briefly faster than TensorFlow on multi-GPU training, then TensorFlow ate the world anyway.
GPT-4 was trained on roughly 25,000 A100 GPUs running for 90-100 days. The electricity alone cost an estimated $63 million — before factoring in failed runs discarded along the way.
AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known protein universe — in under a year. Structural biologists had expected that work to take centuries.

The first neural network to beat humans at Go, AlphaGo, did so in 2016 using a technique Go professionals insisted would never work: valuing board positions with a neural net instead of exhaustive search.
